deck: My First Chess Opening Repetoire - Christof Sielecki

cards.note: the user's own rules for making opening cards
What are the first 2 moves of Philidor's Defense?

front.text: Why does the Philidor Defense have the reputation of being slightly passive?

cards.back:
2...d6 covers the e5-pawn but does not develop a piece and locks in the f8-bishop. Compared to Black's main options, [2...Nc6] or [2...Nf6], the king's bishop can't join the game early on, for example on the squares c5 or b4. Black voluntarily limits their options.

The defense is named after François-André Danican Philidor, the strongest player of the 18th century, who coined the quote 'Pawns are the soul of Chess'.

cards.note: What is your third move against Philidor's Defense?

front.text: Besides attacking the e5-pawn, what does 3.d4 do?

cards.back:
This is White's strongest move. We open the center and prepare the development of the c1-bishop.

[3.Nc3] and [3.Bc4] are good moves that follow basic principles (development), but the immediate 3.d4 exerts more pressure, often leading to an inferior reply.

cards.note: Which 3 Black responses to 3. d4 are most common?
What is your move after 3...Bg4? and why? Black's 2 common responses

front.text: What are all of Black's options after 4.dxe5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Bxf3] Black gives up the bishop pair and speeds up our development, a welcome sight.
- [4...dxe5]? [4...dxe5 | 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 6.Nxe5] is fantastic for White. We win the most important pawn on the board, spoil Black's castling rights, and even win time by attacking Black's g4-bishop.
- [4...Nc6] or [4...Nd7]: in both cases, we can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

cards.note: What are the next 3 plies following 4...dxe5? ?

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nc6 and why?

cards.back: 5.exd6 We can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nd7 and why?

cards.back: 5.exd6 As after [4...Nc6], we can take on d6 and enjoy an extra pawn.

front.text: Why do we recapture on f3 with the queen?

cards.back: We keep our pawn structure intact, and place our queen on an active square. After Black's logical reply, the queen's position will be put to good use: [5...dxe5 6.Bc4] threatens mate.

cards.note: What are Black's 2 most common responses to the checkmate threat 6.Bc4 ?
After 6...Qf6 what are the next 3 plies and what shouldn't White do?
After 6...Nf6 what are the next 3 plies?

front.text: After 7.Qb3!, Black defends the b-pawn with 7...b6?? . What are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
Black can't give up the f-pawn.

- 8.Bxf7+ claude: the f-pawn falls with check.
- 8...Kd7 claude: the king has to step out.
- 9.Qe6# checkmate.

front.text: After 7...Qe7, White has two excellent choices. Which are they, and what does each go for?

cards.back:
7...Qe7 is the relatively best solution, as played in the famous Opera Game.

- [8.Qxb7] wins a clean pawn and secures a large advantage.
- [8.Nc3] is Morphy's move, playing for an attack!

front.text: 8.Nc3 was Morphy's move in the Opera Game. Play his concluding moves after 8...c6.

cards.back:
8...c6 9.Bg5 b5 10.Nxb5! cxb5 11.Bxb5+ Nbd7 12.O-O-O Rd8 13.Rxd7! Rxd7 14.Rd1 Qe6 15.Bxd7+ Nxd7 16.Qb8+!! Nxb8 17.Rd8#

One of the most famous chess games of all time! It's well worth studying in detail.

front.text: What is your move after 3...exd4 and why?

cards.back:
4.Nxd4 An easy move. We recapture the pawn and centralize our knight. A key idea of playing an early d4 is removing the e5-pawn to gain control of this central square for our knight.

3...exd4 is Black's best move. Black has no fully satisfactory way to keep the pawn on e5 and therefore captures our d-pawn.

front.text: What are Black's options after 4.Nxd4?

cards.back:
- [4...Nf6] is a logical choice and the most popular move. Black develops the kingside and attacks our pawn.
- [4...c5]? is dubious. It leads to a structure that we examine via [4...Nf6 5.Nc3 c5], a similar idea.

front.text: What is your move after 4...c5? and why?

cards.back:
5.Ne2 It looks odd, but it follows the same concept as [4...Nf6 5.Nc3 c5 6.Nde2].

claude: Black has weakened the d5-square, and from e2 the knight can reach it via f4.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nf6 and why?

cards.back: 5.Nc3 Easy one: we cover the pawn and develop our knight.

front.text: What are Black's options after 5.Nc3?

cards.back:
- [5...Be7] is Black's best move. Black develops the bishop and prepares kingside castling. It is a modest setup, but Black's position is rather solid.
- [5...c5]? is a mistake, a short-sighted attack on our knight.
- [5...g6], [5...c6] or [5...Nc6] are rare alternatives. Against all these setups, we can play as we do against 5...Be7, by developing our bishop to f4, followed by Qd2 and O-O-O.

front.text: What are the two drawbacks of 5...c5? ?

cards.back:
Black attacks our strong knight, but the cure is worse than the disease. Every pawn move involves a commitment and may weaken crucial squares or pawns.

- The d6-pawn can't be protected by a fellow pawn anymore, and it is a 'backward pawn' on a half-open file. We have good chances to put pressure on the pawn − ideas like a later Bf4 and rooks to the d-file come to mind.
- Even more serious: Black has left the d5-square, a key central point, open for our pieces to use. Black can't control this square with a pawn anymore, and we have excellent chances to establish a strong piece on this outpost square.

front.text: After 5...c5? our knight is attacked. Where does it go and why? Which knight move is less precise?

cards.back:
6.Nde2 We block our own bishop's development, but there is a major upside. Black has weakened the d5-square, which would be ideal for a knight. Our c3-knight is already connected to the square, and from e2 our second knight can quickly reach d5 via the f4-square.

[6.Nb3] is less precise: rerouting the knight to d5 is much more difficult. You could go via b3-d2-c4-e3, which takes ages.

White has a strong alternative in [6.Bb5+], but I prefer the knight maneuver (Nd4-e2-f4) because of its instructional value.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6...Be7?

cards.back:
- 7.Nf4 claude: the knight heads for d5.
- 7...O-O claude: Black castles.
- 8.Bc4 This demonstrates our basic idea. We have full control of d5 and Black suffers due to a bad e7-bishop and a potentially weak d-pawn.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Be7 and what is the plan behind it?

cards.back:
6.Bf4 The most aggressive move. We plan to play Qd2 and O-O-O next. With our king safely positioned on the queenside, we may attack the kingside by pushing our pawns (f3&g4 comes to mind).

White has some good alternatives, in particular [6.g3], intending Bg2 and O-O. Both sides' forces are not in direct contact, which gives us a range of options.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 6...O-O?

cards.back:
6...O-O Black gets their king to safety.

- 7.Qd2 We continue with our plan: secure our king on the queenside and attack on the other side of the board.
- 7...Nc6 claude: Black develops the knight.
- 8.O-O-O We have completed queenside castling and are ready to attack on the kingside.

front.text: After 8.O-O-O, what are the next 3 plies following 8...Nxd4, and what do we play for?

cards.back:
- 9.Qxd4 claude: we recapture with the queen.
- 9...Re8 claude: Black brings the rook to the e-file.
- 10.f3 followed by g4 and h4, the pawn storm on the kingside. It is difficult for Black to generate any counterplay.

front.text: What is our approach against the Philidor's main line (3...exd4), and why does it suit the position?

cards.back:
Black's relatively best option is the capture 3...exd4, leading to the chapter's main line. I suggest aiming for O-O-O here, playing as aggressively as possible. Black's modest setup invites a more ambitious play, which we should happily go for.

The Philidor Defense is fairly unpopular because it is too passive. Black's f8-bishop remains inactive for a while, compared to 2...Nc6, when Black often manages to develop the bishop to a better spot.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Nc6 and why? What other moves are good?

cards.back:
4.Nc3 leads to a position that we investigate via 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4, with a nice advantage.

White has some other good options, like the logical moves [4.Bc4] or [4.Bb5], but playing 4.Nc3 fits best to our concept. 3...Nc6 is much better than 3...Bg4?, but it gives us a wide range of good moves.

front.text: After 3...Nc6, why don't we take on e5?

cards.back:
[4.dxe5 dxe5 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8] is not as promising as it looks at first sight. Black has lost castling rights, but this is less of an issue after queens were traded.

In general, I advise against trading on e5 in this central configuration (e4&d4 vs. e5&d6), as we trade a more active pawn for a passive one and therefore help Black to gain scope for their pieces, in particular the king's bishop, which is limited by the d6-pawn.

front.text: How do we meet Black's rare third moves, anything other than 3...exd4, 3...Bg4 and 3...Nc6?

cards.back: Other moves are rare and best met with healthy development: we play our knight to c3, develop the bishop to c4 and castle kingside next.

front.text: What are the first moves of the Three Knights Game?

cards.back: 3.Nc3 develops the knight and defends e4. Black's best reply is 3...Nf6, entering the Four Knights Game.

front.text: What is Black's best reply to 3.Nc3, and which logical-looking alternative do we look at here?

cards.back:
- [3...Nf6], entering the Four Knights Game. The most popular choice on all levels; masters play more or less only this, as they know the alternatives are inferior.
- [3...Bc5]?! develops the bishop and increases control over d4, so it looks logical, but it has a severe drawback. Your opponents will often choose it.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bc5?! and why?

cards.back: 4.Nxe5! We can take the central pawn, based on the idea 4...Nxe5 5.d4, when the pawn forks bishop and knight and regains the piece. Our knight 'sacrifice' is not a real sacrifice but a trade based on a tactic.

front.text: What are Black's options after 4.Nxe5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [4...Nxe5 5.d4] is the most common. We restore material equality and gain some advantage, but there are a few traps to avoid.
- [4...Bxf2+]?! is dubious but leads to fun complications. Black returns the piece and thus avoids the fork trick.
- [4...Nf6 5.Nxc6 dxc6 6.h3]: White is much better, as Black has no compensation for the pawn.
- [4...Qh4 5.g3] or [4...Qf6 5.Ng4] are easily defused attempts at a Scholar's Mate.

front.text: What do you play after 4...Qh4? and why?

cards.back: 5.g3 An easily defused attempt for a Scholar's Mate. claude: Black threatens ...Qxf2#; the pawn attacks the queen and shuts the h4-e1 diagonal, and we stay a pawn up.

front.text: What do you play after 4...Qf6? and why?

cards.back: 5.Ng4 An easily defused attempt for a Scholar's Mate. claude: Black threatens ...Qxf2#; the knight retreats out of the queen's attack, hits the queen and covers f2, and we stay a pawn up.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Nf6?

cards.back:
- 5.Nxc6 claude: We trade off the attacked knight.
- 5...dxc6 claude: Black recaptures.
- 6.h3 White is much better, as Black has no compensation for the pawn. The same position arises via 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Bc5? 4.Nxe5 Nc6 5.Nxc6 dxc6 6.h3.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Bxf2+?!

cards.back:
- 5.Kxf2 We have to take the bishop, no choice.
- 5...Nxe5 Black restores material equality.
- 6.d4 Completes our dream pawn center and hits Black's knight, winning time.

front.text: After 5.Kxf2, why can't Black give a queen check instead of recapturing with 5...Nxe5?

cards.back:
- [5...Qh4+ 6.g3] claude: the pawn blocks the check and hits the queen.
- [5...Qf6+ 6.Nf3] claude: the knight blocks the check and escapes.

Either way we keep the extra piece.

front.text: After 6.d4, what are White's pluses and problem, and what are Black's 2 most common responses?

cards.back:
We have an excellent pawn center and the pair of bishops, two significant pluses. The problem: our king had to move and looks vulnerable on f2, so we must be careful until it is on a safer spot.

- [6...Qf6+]? is Black's most popular choice, but it is a mistake that only helps us.
- [6...Ng6] is Black's relatively best choice.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Ng6 and why? Which bishop move is less precise?

cards.back:
7.Be2 We must get our king to safety and develop the kingside, so we 'castle by hand': we can't play O-O anymore, but Be2, Rf1 and Kg1 reach the same setup. [7.Bc4] has a similar idea.

[7.Bd3 Qf6+] is less precise, as our d-pawn is hanging.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 7...d6?

cards.back:
- 8.Rf1 Continuing to castle by hand.
- 8...Nf6 Black develops.
- 9.Kg1 Our 'castling by hand' is complete and the king is safe.

front.text: What is your move after 9...O-O? and why?

cards.back: We threaten Bg5 with an annoying pin. After 9...O-O? 10.Bg5, we threaten to destroy Black's kingside by taking on f6, with Nd5 being an additional problem.

front.text: After 9...h6, what is your plan?

cards.back: Black probably needs 9...h6 to stop the pin, but we are in great shape. Bring the queen to the kingside with Qe1-g3, later play Be3, and increase the pressure on the f-file by doubling rooks.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Qf6+? and why?

cards.back:
7.Kg1 The safest spot for our king in the long run. 6...Qf6+? is a very tempting move, getting the queen into the game with a check, but it only helps us.

We have established a perfect pawn center and have the pair of bishops, which is a long-term asset, but our king's safety remains a problem. There are various traps that we need to be aware of. If we navigate these traps, our position will be fantastic: we need to solve the short-term problems to preserve our strategic advantages. Don't be afraid of ghosts!

front.text: What knight moves do we look at for Black after 7.Kg1?

cards.back:
- [7...Ne7] sets a trap, but it is not a great move: if we avoid the trap, Black is stuck with their problems.
- [7...Nc6] is met in a similar way.
- [7...Ng4] is the most dangerous trick that Black has. A rare move, but it can be extremely irritating to face.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Ne7 and why? Why not take the knight?

cards.back:
8.Be3 secures the sensitive a7-g1 diagonal. Finally, we threaten to capture the knight.

We are NOT immediately threatening to capture Black's knight after 7.Kg1! [8.dxe5 Qb6+ 9.Be3 Qxe3#] — a disaster!

front.text: After 7...Ne7 8.Be3, what is your plan?

cards.back: Black has to retreat the knight, when we continue with the plan of Qd2, Bc4 and Rf1. You can also consider playing h2-h4 at some point, getting the h1-rook into action this way.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Nc6 and why?

cards.back: 8.Be3 A good reply, similar to the one against 7...Ne7: it secures our strong center.

front.text: After 7...Ng4, what does Black threaten, and why can't you take the knight?

cards.back:
Black threatens ...Qf2#.

It looks like a blunder, but [8.Qxg4 Qxd4+ 9.Be3 Qxe3#] is a familiar pattern by now. We can't take the knight.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Ng4 and why?

cards.back:
8.Qd2! The only move that works! There is just one move that covers the mate and keeps the d4-pawn protected. The queen must cover f2, and [8.Qf3 Qxd4+] shows the issue with other squares.

The queen is on an odd square and our bishop on c1 is unhappy about the situation, but this is a minor problem. More importantly, we'll send Black's knight back home with h3 next, while Nd5 is looming too.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 8...d6?

cards.back:
- 9.h3 We send Black's knight back home.
- 9...N4h6 claude: The knight has to retreat.
- 10.Nd5 claude: The knight jumps in with an attack on the queen.

front.text: What is your move after 10...Qd8, and how do you continue?

cards.back: 11.Bd3 We have a great position. A way to continue is Qf2, followed by Be3 and Rf1. Black has a misplaced knight on h6, while our knight will find a good route to the kingside via f4.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nxe5 and why?

cards.back: 5.d4 We regain our piece, forking two minor pieces. 4...Nxe5 is Black's best defense.

front.text: What are Black's 2 replies to 5.d4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black's path to a reasonable game is narrow.

- [5...Bd6] is Black's best bet and the only way to reach a playable position, but it is still nice for White.
- [5...Bxd4]? You'll meet this a lot, and we'll get a huge advantage.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Bd6?

cards.back:
- 6.dxe5 We restore material equality, an easy move.
- 6...Bxe5 claude: Black recaptures.
- 7.Bd3 The final move to remember. We develop our bishop and prepare kingside castling, a similar picture as in the main lines of the Four Knights Scotch, which also features the bishop development to d3.

front.text: After 6...Bxe5, why does the bishop go to d3 and not to c4?

cards.back: It looks more active to place it on c4, but after [7.Bc4 Nf6 8.O-O O-O] Black has secured the f7-spot and puts some pressure on e4 (taking on c3 and ...Nxe4 is an idea).

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 7...Nf6, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 8.O-O claude: We castle, as prepared by 7.Bd3.
- 8...O-O claude: Black castles too.
- 9.Bg5 White has a comfortable position. Our pieces are more active than Black's, and we have established an annoying pin. See the game Szwed-Romanishin for more information.

front.text: Black doubles your pawns with 7...Bxc3+. Do you need to worry, and why?

cards.back:
8.bxc3 claude: We recapture.

We don't need to worry about 7...Bxc3+ or similar lines that double our pawns. Black gives up the most powerful piece in return for a weakening of our pawns, which is tough to exploit. Black has no pieces out to attack our queenside pawns while we gain additional possibilities. Later, we might play Ra1-b1-b5 or c3-c4 and Bc1-b2, for example.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Bxd4? and why is it a welcome sight?

cards.back: 6.Qxd4 A welcome sight! Black surrenders the bishop pair and activates our queen. Black has a limited choice now, as we attack the knight.

front.text: What are Black's options after 6.Qxd4, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [6...Qf6] introduces fun complications.
- [6...Nc6 7.Qxg7] or [6...Ng6 7.Qxg7] is simple: both knight moves are blunders.
- [6...d6] is better, but White is in great shape.

front.text: What do you play after 6...Nc6?? and why?

cards.back:
7.Qxg7 is simple. claude: Once the knight leaves e5, the diagonal to g7 is open; we win a pawn and attack the rook on h8.

The same goes for [6...Ng6 7.Qxg7].

front.text: What is your move after 6...d6, and what is the plan? Why not 7.f4 at once?

cards.back:
7.Be3 or [7.Bd2], and White is in great shape. We prepare queenside castling and are ready to attack the knight on e5 with f2-f4 later.

Not at once: [7.f4 Qh4+]! is annoying because we can't play [7.f4 Qh4+ 8.g3 Nf3+]!

front.text: What is your move after 6...Qf6 and why?

cards.back: 7.Nb5! A cool move to remember! We attack c7, but at the same time, the knight does now protect our queen. Black has no good reply now.

front.text: After 6...Qf6, why not attack the queen with 7.Nd5?

cards.back:
Black's last move set a trap. If we'd attack with 7.Nd5??, they have [7.Nd5 Nf3+]!, winning our queen! claude: the knight check uncovers Black's queen on ours.

This is why 7.Nb5! is so strong.

front.text: What are Black's 2 replies to 7.Nb5! and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
Black has no good reply now.

- [7...Kd8 8.Qc5]! is powerful.
- [7...c6 8.Nd6+] and Black's position is lost.

front.text: What is your move after 7...Kd8 and why?

cards.back: 8.Qc5! is powerful. We threaten c7, but also Qf8+!

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 7...c6?

cards.back:
- 8.Nd6+ Much simpler than [8.Nc7+ Kd8], when Black can hope for the ...Nf3+ discovery again. We gain some time with the check.
- 8...Kf8 claude: The king steps out of the check.
- 9.Be3 is allowed thanks to that check. Our queen is secured now against the knight discovery, and Black's position is lost. Our d6-knight is dominating, and their king is stranded on f8.

front.text: What is the conclusion on 3...Bc5?! and what must we put up with in the 4...Bxf2+ line?

cards.back:
3...Bc5 follows general opening principles but has a substantial drawback. We have the strong reply 4.Nxe5!, which often leads to favorable complications.

Some positions are excellent for White, but there are some pitfalls we must avoid. The best example is 4...Bxf2+, which is great for White, but our king is vulnerable. We usually want a safe king, but here we must endure this inconvenience because the upsides (center, bishop pair) are enormous.

That 3...Bc5?! 4.Nxe5! is promising for White is a huge incentive to play 3.Nc3, compared to other options. Black will often get into unexpected trouble.

front.text: Besides 3...Nf6 and 3...Bc5, which 2 Black replies to 3.Nc3 do we look at, and how do we feel about them?

cards.back:
[3...d6] and [3...Bb4], Black's third and fourth most popular moves. They are a welcome sight, as we'll get a promising position without any major effort.

3...Bb4 continues Black's kingside development, a move according to general opening principles. It is still not as good as 3...Nf6, the main continuation: the bishop move has a direct drawback that we can exploit.

front.text: What is your move after 3...Bb4 and why?

cards.back: 4.Nd5! Well, you shouldn't move the same piece multiple times in the opening... unless it is strong! We lose time by moving our knight again, but we will gain MORE time by hitting Black's bishop with pawn moves such as c3 and even b2-b4 and d2-d4 if they retreat the bishop to c5 or a5.

front.text: What are Black's options after 4.Nd5! ?

cards.back:
- [4...Nf6] gets the knight into the game and wants to castle soon, a good move.
- [4...Bc5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4] is a likely continuation, leading to the same position as after 4...Nf6 5.c3 Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.
- [4...Ba5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4]: the same idea also works if Black retreats the bishop to a5, it will lead to the same position.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 4...Bc5, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 5.c3 claude: Prepares b4 and d4.
- 5...Nf6 claude: Black develops.
- 6.b4 claude: We attack the bishop.

After [6...Bb6 7.d4] we have the same position as after 4...Nf6 5.c3 Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.

front.text: What is your move after 4...Nf6 and why? What is a good alternative?

cards.back:
5.c3 Occupying the center by playing c3 & d4 is an attractive idea − let's go for it!

A good alternative is [5.Nxb4 Nxb4 6.d4], opening the position differently.

front.text: What are Black's options after 5.c3, and how do they turn out?

cards.back:
- [5...Bc5] is the most important move to examine. It is played the most here, and the resulting position after our reply may also occur via the move order 4...Bc5 5.c3 Nf6 6.b4.
- [5...Nxd5]?? is a bad one: we attack two pieces and win one of them!
- [5...Ba5] doesn't lose a piece, but it's still a bad move.

front.text: What do you play after 5...Nxd5?? and why?

cards.back: 6.exd5 We attack two pieces and win one of them! claude: the e-pawn hits the knight on c6 and the c-pawn the bishop on b4.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 5...Ba5, and where does the line lead?

cards.back:
- 6.b4 One good reply of many. 5...Ba5 doesn't lose a piece, but it's still a bad move.
- 6...Bb6 claude: The bishop has to move again.
- 7.d4! claude: The same position as after 5...Bc5 6.b4 Bb6 7.d4.

Now [7...Nxe4 8.Bd3 Nf6 9.Bg5] gives White a strong attack. Black has a hard time dealing with the pinned knight.

front.text: What is your move after 5...Bc5 and why? What is a convincing alternative?

cards.back:
6.b4 We attack the bishop again.

6.Bc4 is a convincing alternative, based on [6.Bc4 Nxe4 7.d4 exd4 8.O-O O-O 9.Re1 Nf6 10.Bg5], which gives White a crushing attack. Black's pawn grab 6...Nxe4? is too risky.

front.text: What is your move after 6...Bb6 and why?

cards.back:
7.d4! An important moment. Black's knight currently attacks our e-pawn, but there is no simple solution to this attack. The best solution is ignoring the threat to our e-pawn and focusing on classic opening goals. We occupy the center and don't waste time by covering pawns but rather want to develop quickly.

6...Bb6 keeps the bishop on the most active diagonal.

front.text: After 6...Bb6, Black's knight attacks e4. Why not trade it off with 7.Nxf6+ or cover the pawn?

cards.back:
We could play [7.Nxf6+ Qxf6], but we'd help Black with their development. Moving our knight again is not ideal. On the other hand, we don't want to cover our e-pawn with a passive move.

The best solution is 7.d4!, ignoring the threat.

front.text: After 7.d4!, what do we threaten and what else must Black worry about?

cards.back: We threaten Bg5 and Black also needs to worry about the e5-pawn. There is no good solution for our opponent, and taking e4 is risky for Black.

front.text: After the greedy 7...Nxe4?, what are the next 3 plies?

cards.back:
- 8.Bd3 claude: We develop with an attack on the knight.
- 8...Nf6 claude: The knight goes back.
- 9.Bg5 Black is in trouble. The pin on the knight is tough for Black to handle.

front.text: After 7...Nxe4?, why can't you take on e5?

cards.back: We can't play [8.dxe5 Bxf2+]. claude: the pawn has left d4, so the b6-bishop's diagonal to f2 is open and our king is driven out.

front.text: What are the next 3 plies following 9...h6, and how do we stand?

cards.back:
- 10.Bxf6 claude: We take the pinned knight.
- 10...gxf6 claude: Forced, as 10...Qxf6 loses the queen to the knight on d5.
- 11.a4 A dream position for White. Black's pawns are a mess, and their king can't safely castle kingside anymore. claude: a4-a5 next threatens to trap the bishop on b6.

It's clear that taking e4 is risky for Black.
